rule: An Arabic word always starts with a consonant, followed by a vowel, followed by a consonant: CVC.
A consonant within an Arabic word is followed either by another consonant or by a vowel: CC or CV.
Within an Arabic word, three consonants in a row are not allowed: CCC
Within an Arabic word, two vowels in a row are not allowed: VV
Possible word patterns: CVC + CC + V + C; CVC + CV + CC + V; CVC + CV + CV + C.
Most Arabic words end in a non-pronounced vowel.
ا (alif) has no pronunciation itself; it is either a long “a” or the bearer of ء. ء above ا = a or u, ء below ا = i.
“Ahmed” doesn’t actually start with a vowel but with ء.
Letters are never capitalized.
There's the نسخ (Naskh, printed script) and رقعة (Ruq2ah, handwritten script).

Most words are masculine, except for: female people (“woman”, “mother” …); most countries; most singular words that end in ة (ta2 marbuta); some words connected with the natural world (“wind”, “fire” …); some body parts (“hand”, “leg” …).
Some letters are strong letters. In the Latin spelling they are written as capitals: S (Saad), D (Daad), T (Taa2), Z (Zaa2).
Masculine (muzokkar) words: only add the suffix. Ex. beib → beibei, beibak …
With “esem” we keep the whole stem for ne7na and entoo, to not have 3 consonants following one another.
Feminine (mu2anas) words: add -t and the suffix. Ex. siiyaarah → siiyaartei, siiyaartak …
Words with fat7ah (a) change to kasrah (e) for hiiye and on, to not have 3 consecutive consonants.
Words with kasrah (e) stay as kasrah (e) for hiiye and on.
No definite article needed if there is a possession. Ex. my aunt's house = beit khaaltei, not lbeit khaaltei
No possession for “outside” and “inside”.
Only the last word becomes possessive for “close to” and “far from”.
Combined with noun: before/after + noun Combined with verb: before/after + maa + infinitive, but maa is not negative here. ex. 2abel maa eikul, beshrab = before eating, I drink
“be7aajeh la” (in need of) is the same word for everyone; it’s not a verb.
Words ending in ي (ye/ei) change to “iiyeh”.
Words not ending in ي change to “eh/ah”.
Professions that end with ي (YE/ei), you can use feminine singular for all pronouns except for “he”.
Generally, a strong letter (capital) is followed by -ah, a soft letter is followed by -eh.
Regular rule: drop the last vowel and add -ah or -eh for feminine; drop the last vowel and add -iin for plural.
Irregular rule: drop first vowel for plural (If there's a vowel at the beginning).
If the next word is a noun, we link te marbuuTa (ة) with the next word. if the next word is an adjective, we don’t link te marbuuTa (ة) with the next word.
When using a number with a noun, the noun is either singular, double or plural: 1 → singular; 2 → double; 3-10 → plural; 11 and up → singular.

3-10: take away the ending eh/ah from the number. ex. tleiteh —> tleit fanajiin but add a liaison “e” if the next word starts with a silent letter (i.e., if the second letter of the next word is a consonant instead of a vowel).
11 and up: add -ar to the number. Ex. 7da3sh → 7da3shar Taaleb.
kazaa is always followed by a single of something. Ex. a few cups = kazaa finjein, not kazaa fanajiin.
Everything in nature has a single, a dual, a plural in general and a plural when counting. No liquids, because that we count as “cups of …”.
Plural is always masculine.
motion verbs are always past, present and future
3 verbs are not conjugated as normal but with possessive pronouns as suffix instead: badd (to want), 3end (to have) and fii (can). Ex. anaa baddei, enta baddak, ente baddek …
“fii” without possession → “there is”; “fii” with possession → “can”. Ex. anaa fiinei (I can), fii (there is).
“should” (leizem) doesn’t conjugate in the regular way, but also not with possessive pronouns: it just doesn’t change (anaa leizem, enta leizem, henne leizem …).
The rules for ente, entoo and henne are based on the conjugated version, not on the infinitive.
no swap + no change: buTla3 (to go up) → btuTla3ei / btuTla3oo / byuTla3oo; benzal (to go down) → btenzalei / btenzaloo / byenzaloo
swap + no change: ba3mel (to do/make) → bta3emlei / bta3emloo / bya3emloo; buTbukh (to cook) → btuTubkhei / btuTubkhoo / byuTubkhoo
swap + change u to e: bedrus (to study) → btedersei / btedersoo / byedersoo

The active participle (esme l3aafel, “the name of the doer”) is not a verb but a noun derived from a verb. It describes the state of the doer, and the context of the sentence tells you if it is present continuous, present perfect or simple future. Ex. to write (katab) → one who is writing (keiteb).

Time it refers to, per verb: past, present and future → to go up, to go down, to travel, to write, to come, to return, to arrive, to leave, to talk; past and present → to live; present → to sit; past → to study, to drink, to eat, to pay, to walk, to bring, to be able to, to burn.
There is no “to” in Arabic. To form the infinitive (I ask → I want to ask), drop the first letter of the conjugated verb. Ex. anaa buTlub → baddei uTlub mennek shii.
To form the imperative (gebod) or a polite request, take away the prefix (the first 3 letters). Ex. btetfaDDal → tfaDDal.
The majority of verbs start with “be”. A few more verbs start with “bu”; these are usually followed by a strong letter (capital). Only 3 verbs are conjugated with “ba”.
Verbs ending in “A” (ى alef ma2Suura) change to “EI” (long vowel yaa). Ex. 3aTa → ba3Tei, shtara → beshterei.
Repeating the verb means doing it many times: 7abb → 7ab7ab (to love many times), kabb → kabkab (to throw many times), jarr → jarjar (to drag many times).
“to be” for material things is kein. For non-material “to have”, combine with 3end: kein 3endei (I had), bekuun 3endei (I have), ra7 ykuun 3endei (I will have).
